title: Bias from data
objectives: Spot bias in a chatbot's answers that comes from the examples it learned from.

screens.prose: A firm trains a CV screener on its past hires. Nine of its last ten hires came from Group A. The firm, the groups and the numbers are invented.
screens.question: Trained on these examples, which applicants will the screener tend to favour?

options.text: Applicants who look like past hires, from Group A
The best applicants, whatever their group
options.why: It learned from past hires, not from a measure of who is best. It copies what its examples show.

options.text: Both groups equally, since a computer has no views
options.why: It has no views, but its examples are lopsided, and it copies them.

options.text: Group B, to make up for the past
options.why: Nothing in the examples tells it to make up for anything.

hints.text: What did the screener learn from?
Count the rows marked A.
9 of the 10 examples are from Group A, so "looks like Group A" became a sign of a good hire.

feedback.correct: It favours what its examples show: applicants like past hires.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what pattern the examples show.

explain.text: A model learns the pattern in its examples, as in ai-basics. Here the pattern is "past hires came from Group A". So the screener rewards looking like Group A, whether or not that has anything to do with the job.

screens.prose: A bigger toy version: 100 applicants from each group. Slide between the past hire rates and the rates at which the new model shortlists.
screens.question: What did the model do with the gap in the past data?

options.text: Repeated it: Group A is still far ahead, by even a little more
Closed it, so both groups are now shortlisted at the same rate
options.why: Slide to "Model": 0.33 against 0.09 is a wide gap, not an equal rate.

options.text: Flipped it, so Group B is now ahead
options.why: Group A is still well ahead in both charts.

options.text: Nothing, since the model knows nothing about groups
options.why: It may never be told the group, yet it can learn signs that go with it from the examples.

hints.text: Slide to "Model".
Compare the gap in each chart.
Past: 0.30 against 0.10. Model: 0.33 against 0.09. The gap stays, and grows a little.

feedback.correct: The model repeats the past gap, here a little wider.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the gap between the bars in both charts.

explain.text: The past rates were 30% and 10%; the model shortlists 33% and 9%. It learned the pattern of who was hired, including its gap. These are toy numbers, but the effect is the one to look for.

screens.prose: This is **bias from data**: a model repeats the patterns in its examples, including unfair or out-of-date ones. Both groups have the same number of applicants who meet the job's requirements.
screens.question: How many percentage points apart are the model's shortlist rates for the two groups?

hints.text: Read the model's row.
Group A: 33%. Group B: 9%.
33 − 9 = 24 percentage points.

feedback.correct: 33% − 9% = 24 percentage points, wider than the past gap of 20.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take Group B's rate from Group A's, in the model's row.

byKey.past-gap: That is the past gap, 30% − 10%. The question asks about the model's row.
byKey.ratio: You divided 33 by 9. The question asks how many points apart, so subtract.
byKey.sum: You added the two rates. Take one from the other.

explain.text: The model shortlists 33% of Group A and 9% of Group B, a gap of 24 percentage points. The past gap was 20. Both groups have 40 applicants who meet the requirements, so the gap does not come from the job.

screens.prose: The firm says: "We will fix it with more data: ten times as many past hires, from the same records."
screens.question: Will ten times more data of the same kind remove the bias?

options.text: No: more of the same examples teach the same pattern
Yes: more data always makes a model fairer
options.why: More data sharpens what the data shows. If the past was lopsided, so is the new data.

options.text: It will halve the gap
options.why: Nothing in the new data points the other way, so there is no reason the gap would shrink.

options.text: It will flip the gap towards Group B
options.why: The new records are from the same past, so they lean the same way.

hints.text: Where do the new examples come from?
The same records, with the same past.
Ten times the same lopsided pattern is the same pattern, learned more firmly.

feedback.correct: No. More of the same data teaches the same pattern more firmly.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the extra data shows.

explain.text: A model learns what its examples show. Ten times as many examples from the same past show the same gap, so the model learns it more firmly. Fixing bias needs different data or a different target, not more of the same.

screens.prose: A tool that makes images from text is asked for "a picture of a typical trader". It draws a young man in a suit shouting at screens. This is an invented example.

rows: A picture of a typical trader
A young man in a suit, shouting at a wall of screens

screens.question: Why does it draw this?

options.text: Pictures and text it learned from showed traders that way most often
Because that is what every real trader looks like at work
options.why: Traders are of every age and sex, and most work quietly. The picture shows its examples, not the job.

options.text: Because the request asked for a man
options.why: The request said "a typical trader" and nothing about who.

options.text: By pure chance
options.why: Chance alone would give varied pictures. This one follows a pattern in its examples.

hints.text: Where does its idea of "typical" come from?
Think of films and news photos of trading floors.
Its examples showed traders this way most often, so "typical" means that to it.

feedback.correct: Its idea of "typical" is whatever its examples showed most.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where the picture's pattern comes from.

explain.text: "Typical" to a model means "most common in its examples". If films and photos showed traders as shouting young men, that is what it draws. The output tells you about the examples, not about traders.

screens.prose: Recall l1: a chatbot's text came mostly in a few widely used languages. A firm uses one chatbot to answer customers in several languages.

columns: How much text it learned from

screens.question: Who is likely to get worse answers?

options.text: Customers who write in the rarely written language
Customers who write in the widely used language
options.why: That language gave it the most examples, so its answers there tend to be best.

options.text: Nobody: the same chatbot gives the same quality
options.why: Its quality follows its examples, and they are uneven across languages.

options.text: Only customers who write long questions
options.why: Length is not the issue here; the language is.

hints.text: In which language did it see few examples?
Read the second row.
Few examples, weaker answers: those customers are served worse.

feedback.correct: Customers in the rare language get worse answers: another bias from data.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what few examples did in l1.

explain.text: A model is weaker where its examples are few. A firm using one chatbot for every language serves some customers worse, through no fault of theirs. That is bias from data too, and it should test each language before relying on it.

screens.prose: A manager says: "The screener is a computer program. It has no opinions, so it cannot be biased."
screens.question: What is wrong with this?

options.text: It learned from biased examples, so it repeats their bias without any opinions
Nothing: a program without opinions is neutral by design
options.why: You took "no opinions" as "no bias". The model has no views, but it copies the lopsided pattern in its data.

options.text: The programmers must have written the bias into the code
options.why: No one needs to write it in. Learning from biased examples is enough.

options.text: Programs can be biased, but only very rarely
options.why: A model trained on lopsided examples is biased as a rule, not rarely.

hints.text: Where did the screener's pattern come from?
Compare the model's row with the past row.
It copied the past pattern. No opinion was needed.

feedback.correct: No opinions are needed: biased examples are enough.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where the model's pattern came from.

byKey.neutral: You took "no opinions" to mean "no bias". The model has no views, yet it repeats the gap in the examples it learned from.

explain.text: A model has no opinions, but it learns from examples. If the examples are lopsided, so are its decisions. "It is only a computer" is the reason bias from data goes unnoticed.

screens.prose: In a firm's past records, applicants with a gap of a year or more in their CV were hired less often. Such gaps often come from caring for family or from illness.

rows: A gap of a year or more

screens.question: The pattern is real in the data. Should the screener mark down applicants with a gap?

options.text: No: a real pattern can still be an unfair reason, set by past choices
Yes: the pattern is real, so it is fair to use
options.why: Real in the data is not the same as fair. The pattern may reflect who past managers chose, not who did the job well.

options.text: No: every pattern in hiring data is false
options.why: Many patterns are real. The question is whether acting on this one is fair.

options.text: Yes, as long as applicants are not told
options.why: Hiding a reason does not make it fair.

hints.text: Why might people with gaps have been hired less often?
Read the second sentence of the text.
The pattern may come from past managers' choices about carers and the ill. Copying it repeats their choices.

feedback.correct: Real in the data, and still unfair to act on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where the pattern came from.

explain.text: The pattern is real, but it may record past managers' choices about carers and the ill, not how well people worked. A model that marks gaps down repeats those choices at scale. Check your employer's policy and the law where you work, as well as the data.

screens.prose: A model learns what its examples show: $$\text{the model's pattern} \approx \text{the pattern in its examples}$$ So a gap in the past becomes a gap in the model, and more data of the same kind does not close it.
screens.question: Which change is most likely to reduce the screener's gap?

options.text: Train it to predict who meets the job's requirements, not who was hired
Give it ten times more of the same past hires to learn from
options.why: More of the same examples teach the same gap.

options.text: Use a bigger network
options.why: A bigger network learns the same pattern, perhaps more precisely.

options.text: Hide the group label but keep the same data
options.why: Other details can go with the group, so the pattern can survive without the label.

feedback.correct: Change what it learns from: the requirements, not past choices.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The pattern comes from the examples and what they label.

screens.prose: A lender tests its new credit model before using it. The test applicants in both groups have the same repayment records. The lender and numbers are invented.
screens.question: What is the gap between the two approval rates, in percentage points?

hints.text: Turn each count into a rate first.
70% − 52% = 18 percentage points.

feedback.correct: 70% − 52% = 18 percentage points, for applicants with the same records.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn each count into a rate, then subtract.

byKey.count: That is the gap in approvals, 140 − 104. As rates of 200 each, the gap is 18 points.
byKey.ratio: You divided 140 by 104. The question asks for points apart, so subtract the rates.
byKey.decimal: You gave the gap as a decimal, 0.18. In percentage points it is 18.

explain.text: Group A is approved at 70% and Group B at 52%, a gap of 18 points between applicants with the same records. That is why makers test a model's decisions across groups before use. The lender should find the cause and fix it before any customer is affected.

ideas: A model repeats the patterns in its examples, including unfair or out-of-date ones. This is bias from data.
More data of the same kind teaches the same pattern more firmly. A program with no opinions can still be biased.
A pattern can be real in the data and still unfair to act on. Makers test decisions across groups before use.

formula.name: Bias from data
formula.tex: \text{the model's pattern} \approx \text{the pattern in its examples}
formula.note: Compare rates across groups, not raw counts.

summary.trap: "It is a computer, so it cannot be biased" is wrong. It copies its examples.

quiz.question: A model is trained on ten years of a firm's promotion decisions. What will it tend to repeat?

options.text: The patterns in those decisions, fair or not
Only the fair decisions
options.why: It cannot tell fair from unfair. It learns the pattern of all of them.

options.text: Nothing, since it starts fresh
options.why: It starts from the examples, and learns what they show.

options.text: The opposite of past decisions
options.why: Nothing tells it to reverse anything.

feedback.correct: It repeats the patterns in its examples.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what a model learns from examples.

explain.text: A model learns the patterns in its examples. If past promotions were lopsided, the model's choices will be lopsided in the same way.

quiz.question: A model shortlists 45 of 150 applicants from one group and 15 of 100 from another. How many percentage points apart are the rates?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn each count into a rate first.

byKey.counts: You subtracted the counts. The groups differ in size, so compare rates.
byKey.ratio: You divided the rates. The question asks for points apart.

explain.text: 45 of 150 is 30% and 15 of 100 is 15%. The rates are 15 percentage points apart. With groups of different sizes, compare rates, never raw counts.

quiz.question: Which statement about bias from data is true?

options.text: A model with no opinions can still be biased, by copying its examples
A computer program cannot be biased
options.why: A program that learns from biased examples repeats their bias.

options.text: More data of the same kind always removes bias
options.why: More of the same examples teach the same pattern.

options.text: Removing the group label always removes the bias
options.why: Other details can go with the group, so the pattern can survive.

feedback.correct: No opinions are needed; lopsided examples are enough.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the trap of this lesson.

explain.text: Bias from data needs no opinions: a model copies the patterns in its examples. More of the same data, or hiding a label, often leaves the pattern in place.
